The explorer who reached America in 1492 was Christopher Columbus.

Regarding the interplay between historical context and themes in *The Crucible*, Arthur Miller wrote the play during the 1950s, a period dominated by the Second Red Scare and the political campaigns led by Senator Joseph McCarthy. By setting the drama in the Salem witch trials of the 1690s, Miller created a powerful allegory. The themes of mass hysteria, unfounded accusations, and the abuse of institutional power mirror the tactics used during McCarthyism, where individuals were often accused of communist sympathies without substantial evidence. This historical parallel allows the play to critique the irrationality and moral compromise inherent in both the 17th-century theocratic society and the 20th-century political climate, demonstrating how fear can be weaponized to suppress dissent and destroy reputations.
